common_name: Arctic Fox Rose Foxglove (AAS-Winning First-Year-Blooming Rose-Pink Foxglove)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost for bloom the same year; Arctic Fox Rose is an AAS-winning selection bred for unusually uniform, early first-season flowering compared to older foxglove strains.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil, starting seed early indoors under lights for the most reliable first-season bloom. Arctic Fox Rose is an All-America Selections winner bred for exceptional uniformity and speed to flower, opening dense, upright spikes of clear rose-pink, outward-facing bells with a maroon-speckled white throat several weeks earlier and more evenly than older foxglove strains. Its sturdy, well-branched habit holds up better in wind and rain than taller heirloom foxglove, making it useful in mixed borders and large containers as well as traditional cottage-garden plantings. Deadheading the main spike after bloom often prompts a flush of smaller side spikes, extending the display into summer. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas frequented by children or pets and wear gloves when handling the foliage.
sources: Kieft Seeds — Arctic Fox foxglove series notes

common_name: Dalmatian Series Foxglove (Compact First-Year-Blooming Landscape Foxglove)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost, since Dalmatian needs a longer head start than some foxglove strains to reliably flower the first year; transplant out after frost danger has passed into partial shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil, and keep evenly moist through establishment since this compact series has a shallower root system than taller heirloom foxglove strains. Dalmatian is a vegetatively uniform, dwarf foxglove series bred specifically for landscape beds and containers, topping out under two feet with densely packed spikes of speckled, tubular bells in shades of purple, peach, rose, cream, and white that open reliably the first year from an early sowing. Its compact, self-supporting habit needs no staking and fits smaller garden spaces and mixed containers better than the taller old-fashioned biennial types. In mild climates plants sometimes persist as short-lived perennials or self-seed lightly, though named-series seedlings will not come true from self-sown seed. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so plant away from areas frequented by children or pets.
sources: PanAmerican Seed / Danziger — Dalmatian foxglove series notes

common_name: Profusion Red Yellow Bicolor Zinnia (AAS-Winning Two-Tone Disease-Resistant Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into full sun; this bicolor Profusion selection blooms nonstop from early summer through frost with strong resistance to the powdery mildew and leaf spot that trouble older zinnia varieties in humid weather.

directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep after the last frost in full sun, or set out transplants; the compact, mounded plants need no staking and bloom continuously without deadheading. Profusion Red Yellow Bicolor is an AAS National Award Winner in the popular interspecific Profusion series, opening single, daisy-like flowers with a red outer edge shading into a bright yellow center that shifts and deepens in color as each bloom ages, giving a single plant a naturally multicolored look. Like the rest of the Profusion series, it combines exceptional heat, humidity, and drought tolerance with strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot, making it far more reliable than older tall zinnia varieties through a hot, humid Gulf South summer. Its dense, weather-resistant habit and nonstop bloom suit it well to beds, borders, and containers with minimal maintenance beyond an occasional light feeding.
sources: Sakata Seed — Profusion zinnia series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

common_name: Artisan Soft Orange Coneflower (Compact Vegetative Echinacea with Warm Peachy-Orange Blooms)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Artisan Soft Orange is a vegetatively propagated coneflower bred for a long first-season bloom and improved branching compared to seed-grown echinacea.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid heavy, poorly drained ground where coneflower roots are prone to rot over winter. Artisan Soft Orange is part of a vegetatively propagated coneflower series bred for a warm, soft peachy-orange color that shifts subtly as blooms age, held on compact, well-branched plants that flower more heavily and over a longer season than older seed-grown orange echinacea. Like other members of the Artisan series, it blooms from its first summer and continues through fall, drawing bees and butterflies, with the spent seed heads left standing over winter to feed goldfinches and other birds. Established plants are drought-tolerant once rooted and benefit from being left undivided for several years, since coneflower resents frequent disturbance.
sources: Darwin Perennials — Artisan echinacea series notes

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant once soil has warmed above 70°F, a week or two after the last frost; Mambo's compact 4–6 lb personal-sized melons and relatively short 75–85 day maturity make it a good fit for shorter or more compact garden spaces.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after the last frost, in hills spaced to allow the vigorous vines to sprawl, or trellis to save space. Mambo is an AAS Edible-Vegetable Award winner bred as a personal-sized icebox watermelon, producing dark green, dark-striped 4–6 pound fruit with sweet, firm, deep red flesh and notably good disease tolerance for a home garden variety. Its compact fruit size and relatively fast maturity make it a practical choice for smaller gardens, raised beds, or trellised growing where full-sized watermelon varieties are impractical. Consistent watering through fruit development is important for good sugar content and to prevent hollow heart, and fruit is ready to pick when the tendril nearest the stem browns and dries and the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to creamy yellow.
sources: Sakata Seed — Mambo watermelon variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Watermelon Variety Trials
